newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Port Arthur bereaved vow to move on with life.
newsitem.headline: Port Arthur bereaved vow to move on with life.

text.p: Australians on Monday held a national day of mourning on the anniversary of the country's worst modern-day massacre, as hundreds of people touched by tragedy in Port Arthur sought to repair their lives.

Survivors and family of the victims gathered for an emotional memorial service in the ruins of a 19th century sandstone church at the Port Arthur convict site, where a year ago gunman Martin Bryant murdered 35 people.
"There's a feeling here that this is a very difficult day," Tony Rundle, leader of the island state of Tasmania, told reporters. "But when it's over it's really time to move on."
Only hours before the Port Arthur memorial service, Australian radio reported that Bryant, now serving a life jail sentence, had attempted suicide with an overdose of pills.
Bryant, 29, was found in his prison cell about two weeks ago suffering the effects of an overdose of medication and with a makeshift noose made from torn sheets lying among his bedding.
Bryant is reported to have attempted suicide twice before, but prison authorities decline to call them real attempts to end his own life. Contrition is said to be far from his mind.
"I wouldn't like to assume that this apparent suicide attempt might indicate some act of contrition," said Ian Sale, the psychologist who exmained Bryant before his trial last year.
"I very much doubt that, I am afraid. You don't see redemption being an issue with that particular individual."
Instead, Sale said the anniversary was vitally important to enable people to repiar their shattered lives and move on.
"In life there are various rites of passage we go through," he told reporters at Port Arthur. "The first anniversary is always going to be the toughest."

The nightmare of Port Arthur began on a sunny autumn Sunday when Bryant entered the Broad Arrow Cafe, took a semi-automatic rifle from his sports bag and calmly walked from table to table shooting at point blank range, laughing as he went.

Within 15 seconds, 12 people were dead; within two minutes, 20. The carnage continued outside the cafe, as Bryant hunted down victims at random. Six-year-old Alannah Mikac had run behind a tree when Bryant put the gun to her neck.
"To my darling Lani, I can still hear your voice and smell your hair," Alannah's father Walter wrote on a wreath pinned on Monday to a twisted old gum tree near where she died.
By the time Bryant fled a burning cottage after an overnight siege with police, 35 people were dead, making his killing spree Australia's worst modern-day massacre.
Outrage at the massacre led to tougher gun laws in Australia which now ban semi-automatic weapons like that used by Bryant.
The scars from that bloody Sunday remain raw for the small Tasmanian community, but local community and religious leaders believe time will heal the wounds.

The community has developed close ties with the small Scottish town of Dunblane, hit by an equally devastating tragedy the month before the Port Arthur killings when a gunman shot dead 16 children and their teacher in a school gym.
Teachers and families from Dunblane sent a message to Port Arthur on Monday sharing in its loss and promising to join millions of Australians in lighting a candle for the dead.
Local mayor Neil Noye told around 400 people gathered at the convict church that it was "the anniversary of a day we would like to forget".
"What happened is beyond our understanding...even if we were to know, knowing would not make any difference," Noye said.
Bryant, said to nurse a deep grudge against society, has so far refused to say why he unleashed his shooting spree.
